event.description:
A series of testbeds to prepare operational meteorologists/forecasters to use data from the Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) and the EUMETSAT Polar System Second Generation (EPS-SG) Programmes.
Particular focus is given to the use of novel MTG satellite data from the FCI spectral imager and the LI lightning imager, as well as IRS - infrared sounder. In addition, a range of state-of-the-art nowcasting tools and numerical weather prediction-based guidance will be evaluated.
event.learningOutcome:
The testbeds teach: * Forecasting severe convective storms using state-of-the-art or experimental forecasting tools. * Evaluation of such tools.
At these events, forecasters learn by simulating an operational forecasting situation, making severe weather forecasts and nowcasts using a mix of new nowcasting and forecasting tools, and then evaluating the quality of the forecast and the value of the data and tools.

event.description:
The course focuses on deepening specialist knowledge of satellite meteorology, particularly the use of MTG imagery and products in combination with NWP and other meteorological data. Key subject areas include weather phenomena over the Mediterranean, the westerly wind zone, and Northern Europe, with case studies on wild fires, Storm Amy, and polar lows.
The training is conducted as blended training. Participants will engage in three hours of online work per week, including brief playground sessions, and will attend a four‑day in‑person block to consolidate learning. Learning objectives are to enhance satellite meteorology expertise, improve practical application of MTG data in operational forecasting, and exchange of working methods across weather services. Prerequisites are basic synoptic meteorology, hands‑on forecasting experience, and familiarity with MTG images.
event.learningOutcome: Deepening specialist knowledge in satellite meteorology with focus on MTG combined with other meteorological products (WMO Skills).

event.description:
This course brings together the academic community and National Meteorological Services (NMS) to explore the use of satellite data and Satellite Application Facility (SAF) products in various application areas. Participants will gain hands-on experience in navigating data platforms, accessing and processing satellite data for developing custom applications and research projects.
The workshop will focus on the following topics: * Basics of remote sensing with satellites, data access and handling * MTG FCI RGB images and LI products * Land applications — LSA SAF products * Precipitation and moisture — H SAF products * Atmospheric composition — AC SAF products * Nowcasting — NWC SAF products
A detailed agenda will be available later.
event.learningOutcome: Learning outcomes include enhancing the skills and competencies of young researchers and staff at HNMSs, in the topics related to satellite data exploitation, in order to foster following research and applications of data, as well as supporting cooperation between academia and NMSs.

event.description:
South America is recognized as one of the regions in the world where severe convective storms occur most frequently. These storms are characterized by extreme weather phenomena such as large hail, destructive straight-line winds, tornadoes, locally intense rainfall, and frequent lightning activity.
The 1st South American Symposium on Severe Storms (1st SSTS) will be a scientific and professional event that, for the first time at the continental level, will bring together the scientific and academic community specializing in severe convective storms with professionals from regional, national, and international institutions and organizations, both public and private. These organizations are involved in the monitoring and forecasting of severe storms, as well as in mitigating their socioeconomic impacts across various sectors of society.
In this context, the primary objective of the 1st SSTS is to provide a collaborative forum for the exchange of theoretical and practical knowledge on severe storms across weather and climate timescales, while fostering resilience to these hazardous phenomena, with a particular emphasis on the South American context.
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of the symposium, participants will be able to:
- Discuss the current state of the art in severe storm research, monitoring, and forecasting in South America. - Evaluate recent advances in remote sensing, numerical weather prediction, artificial intelligence, and nowcasting techniques for severe storms. - Interpret case studies of severe convective storms and assess their meteorological and societal impacts. - Exchange best practices for severe weather forecasting, impact-based forecasting, risk communication, and disaster risk reduction. - Strengthen collaboration between the scientific community, operational forecasting centers, government agencies, and industry to improve resilience to severe storms in South America. - Identify emerging research challenges, technological opportunities, and priorities for advancing severe storm science and operations across the region.
event.registrationHowto: https://moodle.cptec.inpe.br/course/view.php?id=42
event.targetAudience: Research staff from research institutes and R&D organizations; faculty members and students from public and private higher education institutions working in Atmospheric and Environmental Sciences or related fields; weather forecasters from national and regional operational forecasting centers; professionals from public and private institutions involved in weather and climate monitoring and forecasting, disaster risk reduction, and emergency response; professionals in civil defense, the electric power, agriculture, aviation and civil and military navigation, insurance, artificial intelligence and applied mathematics, wind engineering, public health, tourism, public policy (social and economic), and technological development; science journalists and professional science communicators; and public decision-makers.
event.title: 1st South American Symposium on Severe Storms (1st SSTS)

event.description:
In partnership with the Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), EUMETSAT offers testbeds to prepare Aviation Forecasters for using data from EUMETSAT satellite programmes in their operations. The FMI aviation testbeds simulate an on-site operational meteorological forecasting environment, enhancing the skills of aviation forecasters in using EUMETSAT satellite data and products in aviation services. FMI will use the GEOWEB environment to run the training testbed, providing the full suite of typical products from models to observations, including, in particular, satellite-based products on icing potential, fog and low clouds, visibility, turbulence, volcanic ash, lightning, etc.
During the testbeds, forecasters first receive theoretical background on the products, then produce on-the-spot forecasts and nowcasts based on selected cases, using a mix of new nowcasting and forecasting tools, followed by a verification and discussion.
Particular focus will be given to the use of MTG-I1 FCI and LI data and products.
The testbeds are part of the EUMETSAT-led user preparation projects for MTG and EPS-SG.
event.learningOutcome: Enhanced skills in using EUMETSAT data and products, in particular those from MTG FCI and LI, to improve aviation weather forecasts.

event.description:
The Trevor Platt Science Foundation (TPSF) and its partners are proud to announce **TREVOR-SAFARI 2026**.
This landmark event merges two major community-building initiatives inspired by the legacy of Prof Trevor Platt, FRS, FRSC. This symposium marks the second instalment of the TREVOR symposium, following its 2023 debut at the Plymouth Marine Laboratory, UK, and the third SAFARI symposium. The previous two SAFARI symposia were organised by ICAR-CIFT (2010) and ICAR-CMFRI (2018).
The symposium is being jointly organised by **TPSF, COD-CUSAT, MBAI, ICAR-CMFRI** and will be held on 4–6 November 2026, at the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (ICAR-CMFRI) in Kochi, India.
The symposium will be preceded by a training course organised by the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS, Hyderabad) and the Department of Chemical Oceanography at Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT, Kochi).
The training course will be run in two segments. The initial segment consists of a series of online lectures, followed by in-person classroom sessions and computer work, from 27–31 October 2026 at INCOIS, Hyderabad, India. The second segment, held in Kochi, India from 1-3 November 2026, consists of a field trip to Vembanad Lake in Kerala, India, and laboratory analyses of the samples collected during the field trip at CUSAT, Kochi, India.
All participants in the training course are expected to submit an abstract to the symposium and actively participate in it.
event.registrationHowto: For more information on how to apply, please visit the [Trevor Foundation 2026 Symposium](https://trevorfoundation.org/symposium) course page.
event.title: TREVOR–SAFARI Symposium 2026
event.titleNative: TREVOR–SAFARI Symposium 2026

event.description: The training will introduce the participants to state-of-the-art satellite remote sensing, ground-based and in-situ measurement techniques for atmospheric composition monitoring and chemical transport modelling in a global context. The course builds on nearly a decade of rich heritage. Past examples of training, including pre-training webinars, can be found at the link below.
event.learningOutcome:
This year the course is focused on the remote sensing of air quality. Key topics will include:
- The recently launched Sentinel-4 and Sentinel-5 missions tools and techniques for retrieving concentrations of pollutant gases from satellites. - Principles of atmospheric chemistry/dynamics and relevance on climate and air quality. - Combining data from different satellite instruments. - Methods underlying how high-quality satellite retrievals can improve the reliability of air quality models and forecasts. - Science communication.
Additional aims include fostering collaboration among participants and encouraging the development of individual and team projects using the data, resources, and methodologies present
event.registrationHowto: Submit your application on the official [website](https://atmostraining2026.esa.int/).

event.targetAudience:
The training is of interest for PhD students, early-career scientists, researchers from academia and research institutes, industry, and anyone interested in atmospheric composition monitoring and modelling. On-site training participation is limited, and selection is competitive.
We are pleased to announce that the webinars prior to the in-person training will be accessible to all. Basic knowledge in the concept of remote sensing and working knowledge of python is expected.
Participants from ESA, EUMETSAT and ECMWF member states are given preference for the in-person training; however, participants from all other countries are also welcome to apply, subject to availability of space.

event.description:
The Short Course on EUMETSAT Active Fire products will take place on Tuesday, 22 September 2026, from 12:30 to 14:00 CEST, during the EUMETSAT Meteorological Satellite Conference 2026 in Darmstadt, Germany.
This hands-on session will introduce participants to active fire monitoring, using Jupyter notebooks to analyse Sentinel-3 NRT FRP, as well as MTG FCI FRP and MTG FCI Fire Temperature products. Attendees will learn how to access, process, and visualise these datasets in order to reproduce the workflow independently after the training session.
Participants must bring their own laptops, and a basic understanding of Python is required.

event.description:
A hybrid event hosted at EUMETSAT, as part of its 40th anniversary, bringing the European Weather Cloud (EWC) user community together to discuss the latest developments, use cases, and future possibilities of the EWC.
Jointly organised by EUMETSAT and ECMWF, the workshop provides an opportunity for users to engage directly with the teams behind the EWC, and with peers who are leveraging this platform for various applications in meteorology, climate, and environmental science. Users from diverse backgrounds, ranging from fisheries and environmental monitoring to weather prediction and AI-driven modelling, will share their experiences, challenges, and innovative solutions developed using EWC. This segment highlights the real-world applications of the cloud.
The full agenda is coming soon.
Attendees can join on-site at EUMETSAT, Darmstadt, Germany, or online. The workshop is open to participants from ECMWF and EUMETSAT Member and Co-operating States.
If you’re interested in presenting your own example of using the EWC, during the next workshops, get in touch with us through our [support portal](http://support.europeanweather.cloud).
event.learningOutcome:
**Stay informed**: Users will get the latest updates on EWC, including new features, capabilities, and plans for the future.
**Learn from real-world use cases**: users will discover how other users are making the most of the EWC for their unique applications and gain inspiration for your own projects.
**Engage with the community**: Users will have the chance to connect with other EWC users, share insights, and find potential collaborators.
**Provide feedback**: Users will be able to share their thoughts with the EWC team to help shape future improvements.

event.description:
Join us as we celebrate 40 years of innovation at EUMETSAT by reviewing our legacy, examining how our environment has changed, and looking forward to what the next 40 years might hold. Expect an evening filled with insights, interaction, as well as a bit of the unexpected.
The Innovation Café is a joint event organised by EUMETSAT and ESOC. This edition is unique as it zooms in on this important milestone in EUMETSAT's history. Come for the ideas, stay for the conversations, and leave with inspiration for what we can achieve with the next 40 years.
The event is taking place after the first day of the EUMETSAT Conference — so if you’re attending, simply continue the conversation with us at the Innovation Café. If you are not attending the conference, we'd still love to see you!

event.description:
Ocean colour observations from Copernicus Sentinel-3 OLCI provide essential information for monitoring marine ecosystems, water quality, biogeochemical processes, and the health of the global ocean. Recent months have seen significant developments to EUMETSAT's Sentinel-3 OLCI marine product portfolio, including updates to processing, new product formats and variables, and an expanding range of tools and user support resources.
This two-hour online event provides a concise update on the latest developments to EUMETSAT's Sentinel-3 OLCI marine products. Participants will gain an overview of recent changes to the operational product suite, including updates to product processing, data formats, marine geophysical products, and access services.
The session will also showcase the latest user support resources available through EUMETSAT, including documentation, software tools, training materials, and practical examples, designed to help users transition to the latest products.
This event is intended for existing and prospective users of EUMETSAT Sentinel-3 OLCI marine products who wish to stay up to date with the latest developments. It will be particularly valuable for participants planning to attend the EUMETSAT Meteorological Satellite Conference, providing an opportunity to become familiar with recent product and service developments in advance of the meeting. Attendees will, therefore, be well prepared to engage with EUMETSAT product experts and take full advantage of technical discussions throughout the conference.
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this event, participants will be able to:
* Describe the recent developments across EUMETSAT's Sentinel-3 OLCI marine product portfolio. * Understand the latest updates to Sentinel-3 OLCI processing, products, and services. * Identify the most appropriate EUMETSAT products and supporting resources for their applications. * Access and make use of the latest documentation, software tools, and training materials. * Engage with EUMETSAT experts and the wider user community on current and forthcoming developments.
event.registrationHowto: [Register](https://eumetsat.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN__oJf_GApQo-mmHxppGJozg) for the event.
event.summary: A two-hour update on recent developments to EUMETSAT ocean colour products, tools and user support.
event.targetAudience:
This course is open to all, but is primarily designed for:
* Established and early career remote sensing researchers with an interest in ocean colour * Private and public sector specialists engaged in marine and coastal monitoring activities * Those attending the EUMETSAT conference who wish to discuss marine applications
event.title: EUMETSAT Ocean Colour: Recent Updates to Sentinel-3 OLCI Marine Products, Tools and User Support

event.description:
The IGAC Early Career Short Course is a 40 person three-day peer-designed course, with hands-on training, on atmospheric chemistry, data analysis, international network building, and soft skills training.
As part of the course, EUMETSAT experts will deliver a three-hour interactive workshop on remote sensing that combines theoretical concepts with practical applications. Participants will gain hands-on experience exploring atmospheric composition data using EUMETView and Jupyter notebooks, through guided demonstrations and interactive exercises, providing a practical introduction to satellite-based atmospheric observations.
event.learningOutcome: * Participants will become familiar with the EUMETSAT data access tools and AC resources. * Participants will learn to use EUMETView in the GUI and through QGIS. * Participants will learn how to visualise a volcanic eruption from space, visualise ash, SO2, and dust plumes, and follow their evolution. * Participants will gain experience in using WEkEO.

event.targetAudience: This course is intended for 'early career researchers', defined for this purpose as PhD or Masters students, or people within three years of graduation from a PhD or Masters programme. Undergraduates, or people not yet enrolled in a PhD or Masters programme, are not eligible.

event.description:
Sea Surface Temperature (SST) and Ice Surface Temperature (IST) products are fundamental to a wide range of applications, from numerical weather prediction and ocean forecasting to climate monitoring and polar research. Over recent years, EUMETSAT has introduced significant developments across its operational temperature product portfolio, including new Copernicus Sentinel-3 SLSTR products, enhancements delivered through the Ocean and Sea Ice Satellite Application Facility (OSI SAF), and an expanding range of user support resources.
This two-hour online event provides a concise update on the latest developments to EUMETSAT's SST and IST products. Participants will gain an overview of recent changes to the operational product suite, including the introduction of new geophysical parameters, such as Sea Surface Temperature at Depth (SSTdepth) and Sea Ice Surface Temperature (IST), alongside updates to processing, product availability, and access services.
The session will also showcase the latest user support resources available through EUMETSAT, including documentation, software tools, training materials, and practical examples, designed to help users transition to new products and workflows with confidence.
This event is intended for existing and prospective users of EUMETSAT SST and IST products who wish to stay up to date with the latest developments. It will be particularly valuable for participants planning to attend the EUMETSAT Meteorological Satellite Conference, providing an opportunity to become familiar with recent product and service developments in advance of the meeting. Attendees will, therefore, be well prepared to engage with EUMETSAT product experts and take full advantage of technical discussions throughout the conference.
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this event, participants will be able to:
* Describe the recent developments across EUMETSAT's Sea Surface Temperature and Ice Surface Temperature product portfolio. * Understand the new capabilities offered by recent Sentinel-3 SLSTR and OSI SAF product developments. * Identify the most appropriate EUMETSAT products, and supporting resources, for their applications. * Access and make use of the latest documentation, software tools, and training materials. * Engage with EUMETSAT experts and the wider user community on current and forthcoming developments.

event.description:
To strengthen the culture of monitoring extreme weather events in Brazil, INPE organizes the Nowcasting Workshops annually. The objective is to train operational meteorologists from civil defense agencies, state and regional meteorological centers, and the private sector in nowcasting—the science of very short-range weather forecasting, which is essential for issuing timely weather watches and warnings.
Held at the CPTEC-INPE facilities in Cachoeira Paulista, São Paulo, the workshops have successfully completed three editions. As a practical outcome, dozens of professionals have been trained and are now equipped to apply state-of-the-art technologies for monitoring severe weather events and supporting operational decision-making.
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of the course, participants will be able to:
- Apply the principles of nowcasting to support very short-range weather forecasting and the timely issuance of severe weather watches and warnings. - Assess the pre-convective environment using sounding data, numerical weather prediction products, and ingredient-based forecasting techniques. - Interpret satellite imagery from the GOES ABI instrument to identify convective initiation, storm evolution, and severe weather signatures. - Analyze lightning observations, including GLM products, to monitor convective development and assess storm intensity. - Interpret weather radar products, including Doppler and dual-polarization data, to detect and monitor severe convective storms. - Estimate precipitation and identify radar signatures associated with hazardous weather phenomena. - Integrate information from numerical weather prediction models, satellite observations, lightning detection systems, and weather radar into a comprehensive nowcasting workflow. - Apply advanced operational tools and techniques through real-world case studies to support decision-making during high-impact weather events.
event.registrationHowto: https://moodle.cptec.inpe.br/course/view.php?id=43
event.targetAudience: Operational meteorologists from civil defense agencies, state and regional meteorological centers, and the private sector. The workshop is intended for professionals and graduate students with a degree in Meteorology or Atmospheric Sciences, or equivalent background, seeking advanced training in nowcasting and severe weather monitoring.

event.description: The course aims to teach participants how to access and analyze fire hotspot and burned area data detected by polar-orbiting and geostationary satellites. The course consists of both theoretical and practical components. The theoretical sessions cover the fundamentals of satellite-based fire hotspot detection, the different types of satellites, the spectral channels used, and burned area mapping. During the practical sessions, participants will use the Python programming language and Google Colab to download, process, visualize, and analyze the data. The practical exercises are based on fire hotspot data processed and freely provided by INPE, as well as burned area data available through the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform.
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of the course, participants will be able to:
- Automatically retrieve fire hotspot data. - Process and analyze fire hotspot data for a selected region. - Create static and animated visualizations of fire hotspots. - Generate statistical analyses and visualizations of fire hotspot data at monthly and annual time scales. - Apply the K-means clustering algorithm to identify the seasonality of fire hotspots. - Analyze satellite imagery for the visual identification of burned areas. - Use spectral indices for burned area detection. - Estimate the extent of burned areas.

event.description:
This training covers the theoretical approaches and key datasets for estimating the near-surface concentration of particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometers in diameter (PM2.5) by using satellite aerosol optical depth (AOD) and other data sources (including ground-based monitors and model estimates).
Participants will acquire knowledge about different methodologies, and their strengths and limitations, for inferring surface PM2.5 from satellite AOD. They will be able to identify access methods for using existing datasets of surface PM2.5 estimated from satellite sensors and other data sources. They will also learn how to compare satellite-based estimates of PM2.5 to in situ measurement data through hands-on coding exercises using a generic code template and suitable co-location methodology. This would be the first step in evaluating the suitability of these datasets for the users’ applications and regions.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training attendees will be able to:
Match the required inputs, strengths, and limitations with different basic methods of inferring surface PM2.5 from satellite AOD.
Differentiate between available data products for surface PM2.5 from NASA and Washington University in St. Louis based on their methodologies, strengths, and weaknesses.
Use NASA Earthdata and the SatPM website to access these surface PM2.5 data products for a location and time period of interest.
Compare these satellite-derived PM2.5 estimates to in situ measurements using appropriate co-location strategies and evaluation metrics.

event.description:
Species distribution models (SDMs), sometimes referred to as ecological niche or habitat suitability models, are a commonly used analytical technique to link known species locations with environmental predictor variables and assess patterns of species occurrence and habitat suitability. SDMs have been successfully used to model the distributions of various species, from butterflies to baleen whales, with a goal of using associations with habitat variables — such as elevation, vegetation greenness, or distance to human settlements — to map the potential distribution to a species across a landscape or seascape.
To implement SDMs, we will fit models using Google Earth Engine (GEE), a cloud-based spatial analysis platform that can simplify the process of accessing and analyzing huge quantities of remotely sensed data.
This course begins by introducing key SDM concepts for participants working in ecology, conservation, or wildlife biology. The course then provides a basic introduction to Google Earth Engine (GEE) and JavaScript coding, before moving on to spatial data manipulation and example workflows for species distribution mapping in GEE.
Participants need no prior experience working with GEE, but we assume participants have a basic understanding of GIS data and concepts, such as rasters (including stacks or multi-band images), vectors, projections, and spatial resolution.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training attendees will be able to:
Conduct basic operations and functions in the Google Earth Engine (GEE) web interface using JavaScript code.
Identify core concepts and applications of species distribution modeling (SDM).
Assess key SDM workflow decisions to ensure occurrence point independence, to select background points, and to choose ecologically relevant predictors.
Access and manage analysis-ready spatial data from the GEE catalog as predictor variables.
Fit species distribution models using machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest) in GEE using a reproducible code-based workflow.
Critically evaluate the appropriateness of the model design and interpret predicted distribution and habitat suitability results.

event.description:
The 7th edition of the advanced IOCCG Summer Lecture Series is scheduled for 5-19 July 2026, in Venice, Italy, hosted by the Institute of Marine Sciences (ISMAR) from the Italian National Council of Research (CNR) and the **[Venice International University (VIU)](https://www.univiu.org/)**. The course will be held at the VIU campus, on the island of San Servolo, located in the Venetian lagoon between the Venice city centre and the island of Lido.
As in **[previous years](https://ioccg.org/what-we-do/training-and-education/lectures/)**, this high-level training course will be dedicated to the fundamentals of ocean optics, bio-optics and ocean colour remote sensing. Several experienced research scientists will provide lectures on cutting edge research, with focus on current critical issues in ocean colour science. Students will have ample opportunity to meet with lecturers for in-depth discussions on various pre-selected topics, as well as on their own scientific research.
Students will learn methods for measuring optical properties and interpreting the results. Practical sessions will also be conducted to help students understand absorption, scattering and the colour of the ocean.
The Summer Lecture Series is an advanced training course targeted at students conducting ocean color research, and is not suitable for beginners with limited knowledge of remote sensing. The course will address theoretical aspects and advanced science questions, rather than practical applications.
event.learningOutcome:
The emphasis of the course will be on current critical issues in ocean colour science, and will consist of lecture-style discussions, with a few hands-on practical and/or field sessions. A range of topics will be covered in the course and will depend upon the expertise of the invited lecturers. Following subject areas will most likely be included (to be updated, once lecturers have been confirmed):
* Inherent optical properties (inversion and applications in coastal and open ocean waters). * Errors and uncertainties in ocean colour remote sensing (emphasis on inverse modelling). * Radiative transfer in the ocean: shallow water remote sensing and HydroLight training. * Ocean colour remote sensing in optically-complex coastal waters. * Atmospheric correction. * Retrieving phytoplankton biomass and functional groups. * In situ measurements.
event.registrationHowto: Applications for the 7th IOCCG Summer Lecture Series are now open. The deadline for applications is 15 February 2026. Applicants will be notified about the success of their application by the end of March 2026. Please see the **[course page](https://ioccg.org/what-we-do/training-and-education/ioccg-sls/)** for more details on how to apply.
event.summary: The 7th edition of the advanced IOCCG Summer Lecture Series is scheduled for 5-19 July 2026, in Venice, Italy, hosted by the Institute of Marine Sciences (ISMAR) from the Italian N
event.targetAudience: The lecture series is open to students from all countries, with no preference for geographical location, however, fluency in English is required. Participants should be familiar with downloading and processing satellite ocean colour imagery, since this is not an introductory training course. The course is primarily intended for PhD students and post-doctoral fellows involved in any aspect of ocean colour research. However, outstanding graduate students with a Masters degree (or studying for their Masters degree), with a strong understanding of ocean colour remote sensing, are also encouraged to apply. Research scientists with more than 10 years of ocean colour research, who are hoping to broaden their knowledge, will also be considered. Once selected, all students are required to attend in person for the full two weeks of the lecture series.

event.description:
Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data is becoming increasingly accessible through open datasets, including those from the newly launched NISAR mission. One of SAR’s main advantages is its ability to observe Earth's surface by day or night and under most weather conditions, making it especially valuable in persistently cloudy regions like the tropics or in high-latitude areas with long periods of darkness.
NISAR provides a wealth of data for both scientific research and practical applications, but it can be challenging for users to interpret and apply. This course is designed to help users understand the unique characteristics of NISAR data and learn how to access, visualize, and analyze them for various scientific and applied purposes.
This training consists of three sessions:
Introduction to the NISAR mission — covering its capabilities and data products, with a focus on amplitude data and its relevance for ecosystem monitoring. This session includes a demonstration of the use of NISAR data for flood detection and monitoring.
Data access and analysis tools — practical guidance on accessing, visualizing, and analyzing NISAR data by using resources available from Earthdata and the Alaska Satellite Facility, as well as ISRO's Bhoonidhi portal.
Interferometric SAR (InSAR) data — for identifying disaster risk areas and assessing damage following extreme events. The demonstration portion of this session focuses on one case study related to identifying areas at risk for landslides and another for assessing earthquakes.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training, participants will be able to:
Identify the characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of NISAR data.
Recognize how NISAR data can be applied to decision-making related to flooding, agriculture, earthquakes, and landslides.
Differentiate between the various NISAR data products and their applicability for different real-world use cases.
Demonstrate how to access NISAR data and tools via the ASF DAAC platform to search, visualize, and analyze data for case studies related to floods, earthquakes, landslides, and agriculture.
Generate a flood map, landslide risk map, and earthquake deformation map for an event of interest using provided Jupyter Notebooks and exporting them into a GIS framework (e.g. QGIS).
Demonstrate how to access NISAR data via the ISRO Bhoonidhi platform, and use available tools for basic visualization and analysis.

Each session will include a 30-minute live Q&A.
Those who attend Sessions 1, 2, and 3 and complete the homework by the due date will receive a certificate of attendance.

Managers from local, state, and federal government and NGOs

event.description:
Cette formation vise à renforcer les capacités des professionnels de la météorologie dans l’accès, le traitement, la visualisation et l’interprétation des données issues du système satellitaire Meteosat Troisième Génération (MTG).
Animée par des experts de la Direction de la Météorologie Nationale (DGM) du Maroc, de Météo-France, de l’EAMAC et d’EUMETSAT, cette formation permettra aux participants d’acquérir une vue d’ensemble des programmes satellitaires d’EUMETSAT et des services de diffusion de données, notamment EUMETView, EUMETCast et l’EUMETSAT Data Store. Le cours présentera les derniers produits du Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) de MTG ainsi que les observations du Lightning Imager (LI), en mettant l’accent sur leurs applications pour la surveillance du temps et la prévision météorologique en Afrique.
Les participants apprendront à accéder aux données satellitaires et à les traiter à l’aide de Python et des notebooks Jupyter. Ils exploreront également la génération et l’interprétation de produits satellitaires tels que les composites RGB, les images « sandwich » et d’autres visualisations dérivées à l’aide d’outils modernes comme Satpy. Grâce à des exercices pratiques guidés, ils produiront des images satellitaires personnalisées, sélectionneront des zones d’intérêt et développeront des chaînes de traitement adaptées à une utilisation opérationnelle des données satellitaires.
Afin d’illustrer la valeur opérationnelle des observations MTG, les participants analyseront des études de cas météorologiques et mettront en pratique les compétences acquises pour soutenir les activités de prévision météorologique et de surveillance environnementale.
event.host: General Directorate of Meteorology of Morocco
event.learningOutcome:
Au terme de cet atelier, les participants seront capables de :
* Comprendre les mécanismes généraux de diffusion des données satellitaires d'EUMETSAT.
* Maîtriser et utiliser de manière autonome les outils dédiés à l'accès, au traitement et à la visualisation des données satellitaires pour un usage météorologique opérationnel.
* Manipuler et exploiter efficacement les données satellitaires afin de mener des analyses météorologiques précises et de soutenir la recherche appliquée.
* Concevoir et développer des supports pédagogiques en météorologie satellitaire, notamment à travers l'élaboration d'études de cas concrètes pour la formation.
* Intégrer de façon opérationnelle les méthodes et les produits satellitaires au sein de leurs activités météorologiques quotidiennes.

event.description:
The Ocean surface topography science team meeting (OSTST) is a joint endeavour between EUMETSAT, the European Space Agency, CNES (France’s space agency), NASA, NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), with EU funding through its Copernicus programme.
Experts from around the world will gather to discuss the performance of current satellite altimetry constellations, as well as the use and information-sharing about all present, past, and future altimeter missions. While most applications focus on the open oceans, there will also be an emphasis on coastal areas, polar seas, and inland waters.
In addition, and following on from the successful launch of the Copernicus Sentinel-6B satellite in November 2025, this OSTST meeting will place a strong focus on the commissioning status and activities of the mission.
It will take place jointly, with meetings dedicated to the Sentinel-6B validation team and the international DORIS service, where teams will report on the findings from the satellite’s commissioning.

event.description:
Floods are the most common and widespread of all weather-related natural disasters. Lasting from minutes to weeks, floods can place a huge burden on a community, including loss of life, damage to infrastructure and economies, and long-term impacts on human health and well-being. Remote sensing observations and Earth system models, when combined with hydrologic models, can support both flood monitoring and prediction efforts to significantly improve preparedness and response planning.
This three-part training includes an overview and demonstration of flood monitoring tools based on remotely sensed optical observations, NASA's near real-time Global Flood Product, and several Observational Products for End-users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA). Additionally, the training introduces a streamflow prediction tool — the Group on Earth Observations Global Water Sustainability (GEOGLOWS) model — which provides global, historical, and 15-day streamflow predictions. Trainers guide participants through hands-on exercises to access and visualize selected flood data.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training attendees will be able to:
Identify datasets in NASA's Global Flood Product, which is based on remotely sensed optical observations.
Use the webtool, NASA Worldview, to access and visualize flooded regions from Global Flood Product, available from multiple satellites, from 2021 to near-real time.
Identify OPERA dynamic surface water extent data for flood detection derived from optical and SAR observations.
Access and visualize OPERA dynamic surface water extent data for flood events using NASA Worldview.
Identify the capabilities of GEOGLOWS River Forecast System (RFS) for global streamflow prediction.
Use GEOGLOWS Hydroviewer to access globally available retrospective and predicted streamflow for selected rivers.

event.description:
The European Weather Cloud (EWC) teams at ECMWF and EUMETSAT are pleased to invite you to the second thematic EWC webinar of 2026.
These recurring thematic webinars are aimed at all users of the EWC service, provided by EUMETSAT and ECMWF, which is available to all ECMWF and EUMETSAT Member and Co-operating States. Our primary objective is to provide guidance to users on how to effectively use the different capabilities of the EWC.
Information on the previous webinars, including their recordings, can be found [on the ECMWF confluence site](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/EWCLOUDKB/EWC+Training+and+Tutorials).
In this webinar, we will focus on the transition away from Morpheus, which will be phased out at the end of 2026. We will show how users can now perform the same tasks using the new EWC services, including OpenStack Horizon, the EWC Community Hub, and the EWC Identity and Access Management (IAM) service.
By the end of this session, participants will have a clear understanding of how to carry out the most common activities on the EWC using the new, harmonised set of services available (which will be released in the next months) across both EUMETSAT and ECMWF.
event.learningOutcome:
Participants will learn how to:
* Understand how the new services fit together and how the overall user experience differs from the Morpheus‑based workflow. * Use OpenStack Web and CLI to perform the key operations that were previously done in Morpheus, such as backups. * Use the EWC Community Hub to discover, deploy, and reuse community‑maintained items that replace or improve workflows previously implemented through Morpheus blueprints or instances.
event.registrationHowto:
This webinar is open to anyone from an ECMWF or EUMETSAT Member and Co-operating State.
If you would like to attend the webinar, please [complete the registration form](https://events.ecmwf.int/event/564/registrations/436/). We will alert you of your acceptance to the webinar and send you all the joining information and Microsoft Teams meeting details in due course.

event.description:
Extreme heat events are defined as prolonged periods of excessively high temperatures for multiple consecutive days. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), heat stress is the leading cause of weather-related deaths and can exacerbate accidents, underlying illnesses, and the transmission of some infectious diseases. This intermediate-level training equips participants with the foundational theory and practical skills to leverage thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing to quantify these risks.
The course begins by establishing the physical principles of TIR, including emissivity and blackbody radiation. While these fundamentals are broadly applicable to numerous applications, this training specifically focuses on using data from NASA’s Ecosystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (ECOSTRESS) to identify heat-vulnerable communities and quantify urban heat island (UHI) effects.
In the hands-on component, participants will process ECOSTRESS Land Surface Temperature (LST) data in R – including quality filtering and time-of-day subsetting – and apply the interactive ECOSTRESS LST Downscaling Tool in Google Earth Engine. This tool uses a random forest model to enhance spatial resolution from 70 m to 10 m, translating satellite observations into street-scale thermal maps suitable for urban planning, strategic greenspace placement, and extreme heat early warning systems.

event.description:
This year, the 57th International Liège Colloquium on Ocean Dynamics will focus on submesoscale processing in the ocean.
The ocean is rich in processes that manifest at scales between hundreds of metres and tens of kilometres, small enough for the constraints of the Earth’s rotation and oceanic stratification to be overcome, but larger than that of three-dimensional turbulence. Where multiple forces in the ocean (Coriolis force versus advection and buoyancy versus shear stress) are of similar importance, we witness a wide range of dynamic instabilities that respond to surface forcing and boundary stresses, and interact with the mesoscale flow field, upper ocean turbulence, and near-inertial waves. These dynamics result in enhanced vertical velocities and mixing, as well as stratification, on time scales that range from a few days to the inertial period, and intersect with the timescales of internal waves and tides.
Their diagnosis is facilitated through advances in high-resolution autonomous, in-situ, and remotely-sensed observations, modelling, and theoretical advances. Their implications are wide-ranging, and include the transfer of energy across scales, lateral mixing and transport, restructuring of the upper ocean’s density and stratification, modulation of air-sea, ice-ocean, ocean-bathymetric interactions, the exchange of biogeochemical properties across the mixed layer base, subduction of surface water, and export of particulate organic carbon and oxygen from the surface mixed layer. The similarity of physical and biological time scales of phytoplankton growth heightens the relevance of submesoscale processes for the production and export of phytoplankton, and the structuring and diversity of oceanic ecosystems.
By revisiting this topic, 10 years after the 48th Liège Colloquium, this edition aims to assess the new developments in submesoscale research, across a range of oceanographic disciplines, including observational (in situ and remote sensing), modelling (dynamic and deep-learning based) and theoretical approaches. Topics that will be addressed include:
* Dynamics and impacts of frontal and mixed-layer instabilities, including, but not limited to baroclinic instability, symmetric instability, inertial instability, and ageostrophic anticyclonic instability. * Interactions between surface boundary layer turbulence and submesoscale instabilities derived from large-eddy simulation and observations. * Submesoscale air-sea interaction, including air-sea exchange at the submesoscales and its impact on boundary layer coupling. * The role of submesoscales in vertical exchanges between the ocean surface layer and the ocean interior, including leading order processes, implications and progress towards parameterisation. * Surface signatures of submesoscale dynamics from remotely sensed surface topography, roughness, and ocean color. * Mesoscale-submesoscale interactions, energy cascades, cross-scale interaction. * Physical-biological interactions and implications for biogeochemistry, productivity, export, and ecosystem structure and diversity. * Lateral stirring and transport by submesoscale turbulence. Cross frontal exchange and implications for freshwater transport and ecosystem dynamics. * Coastal and high latitude submesoscale dynamics, prediction improvement, coastal resilience. * Submesoscales in the bottom boundary layer and interactions with topography. * Frontal-wave interaction at submesoscales, internal wave modification and trapping, internal wave generation at submesoscales. * Modelling issues related to multi-scale and multi-physics nature of the processes and in particular model nesting, unstructured grids, developments of new discretisation schemes and the use of machine learning. * Submesoscales and climate including progress on parameterisations, the response of submesocales to long-term climate forcing and the influence of submesoscales on the equilibrium state of the ocean on longer timescales.

Please note that **abstract submission closes on 31 January**.

event.description:
NASA's Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) lidar mission provides an extensive global sample of forest structure measurements and high-quality biomass estimates. Applying these measurements to practical carbon accounting requires extending mapped biomass information back in time so that current carbon gains under present management can be compared to past trends.
This intermediate-level training introduces key concepts in carbon monitoring, including system requirements, decision-making needs, and the concept of additionality. Participants learn how the OBIWAN application builds on GEDI’s model-based statistical framework and underlying data infrastructure to generate biomass change estimates, along with associated uncertainties, for user-defined areas and time periods. The training also covers validation approaches, including the use of U.S. Forest Service inventory data to assess the accuracy and precision of OBIWAN outputs.
Through hands-on activities, participants apply GEDI-based estimation methods, visualize footprint and gridded biomass products, and use the OBIWAN API to generate and analyze biomass change. Participants also explore how to compare carbon gains against business-as-usual scenarios, supporting practical, repeatable forest carbon monitoring and decision-making.

event.description:
This “HIW course” is an online course for EUMETCAL and will focus on the use of a particular forecasting method based on Doswell’s ingredient-based forecasting method IBM (1996). This method assumes that three ingredients are needed for convection: moisture, lift, instability (and vertical wind shear to take the modes in convection into account).
These convection modes each have their own distinctive characteristics as regards duration, radar images and, in particular, hazardous weather phenomena (lightning, wind gusts, hail and heavy precipitation). This method has been incorporated into a convection scheme that is currently used at the KNMI forecasting office; it leads, via a few steps, to one of four convection modes. This course e.g. explain the method and describe a number of typically synoptic situations that yield severe convection with some regularity.
The use of the convection prediction scheme in forecasting convection leads to a better physical understanding of convection, more objective forecasting methodologies and more accurate forecasts of hazardous weather phenomena. The convection prediction scheme can be used to make a good assessment of the probability of hazardous weather phenomena. The latter are rare in the case of single cells, for example, whereas pulse storms are frequently accompanied by strong downdrafts (wind gusts) and heavy precipitation and supercells are infamous for their prolonged duration, large hail, strong lightning activity and wind gusts.
On completion of this course, participants will be able to: - determine where and when deep convection will be initiated using the convection scheme (IBM), - find the overlapping regions of moisture, instability and lift, - determine the type of convection to expect: single cell/pulse cell, multi-cell, squall line or supercell, - determine the corresponding hazardous weather.

event.description:
Groundwater is a vital resource, especially in arid regions where surface water is limited. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) reports approximately 82 billion gallons of groundwater are withdrawn daily in the U.S. for domestic, irrigation, industrial, mining, thermoelectric, livestock, and aquaculture uses.
According to the National Groundwater Association (NGWA), groundwater accounts for about 29% of total U.S. water usage; about two thirds of that groundwater is used for irrigation. Aquifers in certain regions of the world are being depleted by unsustainable groundwater pumping to support irrigated agriculture, including in southern High Plains and Central Valley aquifers in the U.S., northern India, the North China Plain, and parts of the Middle East.
The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE, 2002–2017) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO, 2018–present) satellite missions -- supported by NASA and the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) -- provide monthly estimates of changes in terrestrial water storage (the sum of groundwater, soil moisture, surface waters, snow, and ice) at spatial resolutions no better than about 150,000 km² at mid-latitudes. While useful for detection of large-scale changes, the coarse resolution limits regional-scale groundwater assessments.
There are, however, groundwater products with higher spatial resolutions, which can be useful for finer scale groundwater monitoring. A new product from Observational Products for End-Users from Remote Sensing Analysis (OPERA), provides surface displacement products (DISP) for North America indicating subsidence due to groundwater withdrawal based on Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) from Sentinel-1 at 30 m2 (and from NISAR as of next year). In addition, NASA's Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) assimilates GRACE/GRACE-FO data into a land surface model along with other, higher resolution inputs, producing daily outputs on a 0.25° (~25 km) grid.
This three-part training will focus on an overview of GRACE/GRACE-FO data, OPERA-DISP data, and GLDAS groundwater data for assessing seasonal to interannual groundwater changes at various spatial scales. The training will provide hands-on experience in accessing and analyzing these products for applications.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training attendees will be able to:
Identify characteristics of groundwater quantity datasets from GRACE/FO, OPERA, and GLDAS.
Access, analyze, and visualize GRACE/FO data to monitor seasonal to interannual changes in large-scale total terrestrial water storage.
Access, analyze, and visualize GLDAS data to monitor seasonal to interannual changes in groundwater using at regional scale.
Map surface subsidence related to groundwater extraction with OPERA Displacement (DISP) data.
Utilize groundwater products from these datasets at multiple spatial/temporal scales to make decisions in a variety of applications, such as monitoring drought and flood conditions, planning groundwater resources for irrigation.

event.description:
In partnership with the Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), EUMETSAT offers testbeds to prepare Aviation Forecasters for using data from EUMETSAT satellite programmes in their operations. The FMI aviation testbeds simulate an on-site operational meteorological forecasting environment, enhancing the skills of aviation forecasters in using EUMETSAT satellite data and products in aviation services. FMI will use the GEOWEB environment to run the training testbed, providing the full suite of typical products from models to observations, including satellite-based products on icing potential, fog and low clouds, visibility, turbulence, volcanic ash, lightning, etc.
During the testbeds, forecasters first receive theoretical background on the products, then produce on-the-spot forecasts and nowcasts based on selected cases, using a mix of new nowcasting and forecasting tools, followed by a verification and discussion.
Particular focus will be given to the use of MTG-I1 FCI and LI data and products.
The testbeds are part of the EUMETSAT-led User Preparation projects for MTG and EPS-SG.

event.description:
This “HIW course” is an online course for EUMETCAL and will focus on the use of a particular forecasting method based on Doswell’s ingredient-based forecasting method IBM (1996). This method assumes that three ingredients are needed for convection: moisture, lift, instability (and vertical wind shear to take the modes in convection into account).
These convection modes each have their own distinctive characteristics as regards duration, radar images and, in particular, hazardous weather phenomena (lightning, wind gusts, hail and heavy precipitation). This method has been incorporated into a convection scheme that is currently used at the KNMI forecasting office; it leads, via a few steps, to one of four convection modes. This course e.g. explain the method and describe a number of typically synoptic situations that yield severe convection with some regularity.
The use of the convection prediction scheme in forecasting convection leads to a better physical understanding of convection, more objective forecasting methodologies and more accurate forecasts of hazardous weather phenomena. The convection prediction scheme can be used to make a good assessment of the probability of hazardous weather phenomena. The latter are rare in the case of single cells, for example, whereas pulse storms are frequently accompanied by strong downdrafts (wind gusts) and heavy precipitation and supercells are infamous for their prolonged duration, large hail, strong lightning activity and wind gusts.
On completion of this course, participants will be able to: - determine where and when deep convection will be initiated using the convection scheme (IBM), - find the overlapping regions of moisture, instability and lift, - determine the type of convection to expect: single cell/pulse cell, multi-cell, squall line or supercell, - determine the corresponding hazardous weather.

event.description:
Building on the foundations introduced in the first session (10 March 2026), this second online session is designed as an expert-level course, focusing on more advanced scientific concepts and hands-on data analysis workflows for fire monitoring and impact assessment.
The course begins with a deeper theoretical overview of fire processes, atmospheric aerosols, and burned area dynamics. Participants will explore the physical principles behind Fire Radiative Power (FRP), aerosol transport, and post-fire landscape changes.
Following the theoretical introduction, the session will move into a series of live demonstrations using Jupyter Notebooks within the WEkEO environment, showcasing practical workflows for accessing, analysing, and visualising Copernicus data.
Participants will:
- Work with Sentinel-3 FRP data to monitor active fire intensity and temporal evolution.
- Explore Sentinel-3 Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) products to assess smoke plume dispersion and atmospheric impacts.
- Use a dedicated Sentinel-2 notebook, applying the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) to map and analyse burned areas after a fire event.
Through these guided exercises, attendees will follow a complete workflow from data access to interactive analysis, gaining practical experience with advanced EO tools commonly used in fire science and operational monitoring.
This expert course complements the first basic session by moving beyond visualisation into quantitative analysis, enabling participants to better understand fire behaviour, atmospheric effects, and post-fire impacts using satellite data and cloud-based platforms.
Resources available here -> https://classroom.eumetsat.int/course/view.php?id=600
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of the session users should be able to:
- Explain advanced concepts related to fire dynamics, aerosols, and burned area processes, and their impacts on the atmosphere and land surface. - Interpret Fire Radiative Power (FRP) data from Sentinel-3 to analyse active fire intensity and temporal evolution. - Analyse Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) products from Sentinel-3 to assess smoke plume transport and atmospheric effects. - Apply Sentinel-2 Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) techniques to map and evaluate burned areas following wildfire events. - Use Jupyter Notebooks within the WEkEO environment to access, process, and visualise EO fire-related datasets, following complete analysis workflows.

event.description:
This first session of the two-part webinar series builds a foundational understanding of fires, remote sensing principles, and key Earth Observation products to support more advanced analysis in part 2.
The session begins with a brief introduction to fire behaviour and dynamics; setting the scene by exploring the environmental relevance of wildfires, and focusing on the role of satellite observations in fire detection and monitoring. An overview of the main satellite missions and fire-related products will be presented to support this fundamental knowledge.
Participants will then follow a guided demonstration using EUMETView, EUMETSAT’s user-friendly visualisation platform, to identify and explore a real fire event. The demonstration will include:
- Sentinel-3 OLCI RGB imagery to observe smoke plume development and surface features. - Sentinel-3 SLSTR Fire Radiative Power (FRP) products to detect active fires and assess their intensity. - MTG Fire Temperature RGB data to illustrate fire intensity.
By combining these datasets, participants will see how different satellite sensors work together to provide a view of fire activity and plume evolution.
The session concludes with a summary of key resources and guidance for further exploration of fire products and visualisation tools.
This first session lays the groundwork for the second, which will move beyond the basics into more advanced fire monitoring, analysis techniques, and practical workflows.
Resources available here -> https://classroom.eumetsat.int/course/view.php?id=600
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of the session, users should be able to:
- Explain the basic principles of wildfire behaviour and the role of satellite remote sensing in detecting, monitoring, and observing fires.
- Identify key Earth Observation fire products used for monitoring active fires and smoke plumes, such as RGB imagery and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).
- Use EUMETView to visualise a fire event, generating images or animations to observe fire activity and plume evolution.
- Recognise key resources and tools for further exploration of fire data following the course.

event.description:
The Meteosat Third Generation Lightning Imager (MTG-LI) has been operational since 31 October 2024. MTG-LI enables the monitoring of lightning activity from global scales down to single storms. During the year 2025, it observed 608 million lightning flashes, providing users with the most complete characterization of total lightning activity over Europe, Africa, most of the Atlantic Ocean, and parts of South America, the Indian Ocean, and the Middle East. The presentation will illustrate key properties of the lightning activity observed by MTG-LI over the whole year of 2025 including global-scale statistics, regional and high-latitude storm monitoring, and flash level details that the instrument is able to resolve.
This webinar will be presented by Sven-Erik Enno (EUMETSAT) on 10 March 2026 at 12:00 UTC / 13:00 CET.

event.description:
Land cover and land use change (LCLUC) describes the many ways our world changes around us. Every new building, each vacant lot, and the expansion and retreat of forests or wetlands are all examples of LCLUC. These changes may be slow or sudden, but understanding the ways in which our landscape is changing gives us the opportunity to better anticipate and avoid problems that may arise.
This training, led by NASA's Applied Remote Sensing Training program (ARSET), covers some of the ways that we can use NASA data to determine what is happening on the ground and how that changes over time. Participants will see examples of supervised and unsupervised classification models implemented in the R statistical coding language, and improve their understanding of how these models can be used to produce maps and metrics of LCLUC.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training, attendees will be able to:
Access NASA Earth observation data (e.g., Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS)) relevant to LCLUC mapping.
Convert NASA Earth observation data into distinct land cover and land use (LCLU) classes using supervised and unsupervised machine learning classification methods in the R programming language.
Recognize the role of classification methods as one part of a change monitoring strategy.
Compute a change matrix representing the change in LCLU between two dates.
Create a map in RStudio visualizing the differences in LCLU between two dates.
event.registrationHowto: Please register here: https://go.nasa.gov/4s2XnyJ
event.targetAudience: Professionals interested in coding to quantify land cover change as it relates to phenomena such as forest composition change, deforestation, urban expansion, habitat loss, and hydro/cryosphere changes. Other scientists or analysts interested in leveraging automated tools for decision support around land use management, natural resource management, or other issues that have an impact on how our world is structured across space and time.
event.title: Visualizing Land Cover and Land Use Change with NASA Satellite Imagery
event.titleNative: Visualizing Land Cover and Land Use Change with NASA Satellite Imagery

event.description:
As part of these events, the Atmospheric Composition team at EUMETSAT will host two sessions:
Session 1: Fire hotspots and smoke monitoring with Sentinel-3: basic concepts - Date: 24 February - Session length: ~20 minutes - Session type: Theory
This first session provides a theoretical introduction to wildfire activity in Spain and Europe in 2025, setting the environmental context and explaining the role of satellite Earth Observation in detecting and monitoring fires. Participants will be introduced to Copernicus fire-related data products, with a focus on Sentinel-3 Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) and Fire Radiative Power (FRP). This session lays the conceptual foundation for the hands-on demonstration that follows.
Session 2: Fire hotspots and smoke monitoring with Sentinel-3: Tutorial - Date: 26 February - Session length: ~30 minutes - Session type: Jupyter Notebook demonstration
The second session is a practical, hands-on demonstration, focused on working with real wildfire data. Using a Jupyter Notebook, participants will follow a step-by-step walk-through, showing how to access, process, and visualise fire-related datasets. The session includes: - A live demonstration of data access using WekEO HDA through a Jupyter Notebook. - Practical processing and visualisation of S3 AOD and S3 FRP data through a Jupyter Notebook.
Participants will gain a clear understanding of how the WEkEO platform can be used to support wildfire analysis and monitoring.
event.learningOutcome: - Users will familiarise themselves with EUMETSAT in the general EO business. - Users will find out which fire-related data are available from EUMETSAT/Copernicus services. - Users will able to familiarise themselves with EUMETSAT Atmospheric Composition Jupyter Notebooks, and use WEkEO as a tool.

event.description: In early 2026, EUMETSAT will be running the next iteration of the 'Supporting Marine Earth Observation Applications (SMA)' course. The course introduces our marine data catalogue and aims to help you develop workflows that support your own application-specific goals. If you wish to learn about, or work more extensively with our satellite-derived, ocean colour, sea surface temperature, altimetry, sea ice, or wind data, then we encourage you to apply. This year, the course will be delivered in partnership with the **Deutsches Geodätisches ForschungsInstitut (DGFI) at the Technical University of Munich**, and we particularly welcome applications from those who are interested in working with altimetry. During this course you will learn how to independently access and process data from the EUMETSAT product catalogue for your marine workflows and applications. The focus will be on data streams from EUMETSAT Copernicus marine missions (Sentinel-3, Sentinel-6) and derived downstream products, those derived from Copernicus supporting missions, and those made available by the Ocean and Sea Ice Satellite Application Facility (OSI SAF). Training will take place entirely online, in two phases, which will be supported by experts in the relevant fields: * The first, self-paced phase will take place between 23 February and 13 March 2026 and will take approximately nine-15 hours to complete. It will involve self-paced flexible learning through webinars, forums, and technical checks (particularly for software installations), documentation, and assignments. * The second, virtual classroom phase will be take place between 16 March and 20 March 2026, using GatherTown and other collaborative tools. This phase will be made up of interactive tutorials, live demos, group work, and 1:1 meetings. During this intensive week, which will require five-eight hours of participation each day, we will focus on co-creating a **mini-project** directly relevant to your application of interest. During the course, you will: * Learn about the specifics of the marine products that EUMETSAT provides (variables, timeliness, resolution, data formats). * Select appropriate products from the EUMETSAT marine catalogue and access them using GUI-based and automated services. * Use relevant software tools, such as SNAP, and scripting languages, such as Python, to acquire, visualise and process Earth observation data from multiple sources. * Work with trainers to design workflows around these products and tools, tailoring approaches to the specific needs of your participant-defined application.
event.learningOutcome:
Participants completing this course will:
* Learn about the operational role EUMETSAT plays in marine Earth observation, understand the range of products it provides and appreciate how it supports downstream services. * Be able to select and download the appropriate data for their marine application of interest. * Be able to manipulate these products for their own purposes, using appropriate software packages and code-based approaches. * Produce a use case specific to their needs, in collaboration with other participants and trainers.
event.registrationHowto: A limited number of places are available on this course. Visit the “Apply for courses” section of our course Moodle page for more information on how to apply.

event.description:
Monitoring water quality is vital for managing drinking water treatment and public health and ecosystem advisories. In particular, monitoring harmful algal blooms and water transparency are crucial for assessing health and productivity of freshwater and saltwater fisheries. Conventional in situ measurements of water quality parameters are expensive and have limited spatial and temporal coverage. Remote sensing provides a cost-effective way to assess water quality in thousands of lakes and on coastal waters.
NASA has developed the Satellite-based Tool for Rapid Evaluation of Aquatic Environments (STREAM) — an interactive web tool that enables high-resolution (20–30 meter) monitoring of water quality in inland lakes and coastal waters across the U.S. and selected other countries. STREAM provides both past (since 2018) and near real-time maps of chlorophyll-a concentration, Secchi disk depth, and total suspended solids based on data from the Landsat 8/9 Operational Land Imager (OLI) and the Sentinel 2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI). Additionally, an open-source machine learning model based on a Mixture Density Network (MDN) is available to estimate water quality parameters for any inland or coastal water body worldwide (minimum size: 100m x 100m).
This two-part training led by NASA's Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET) introduces the STREAM web tool to visualize maps of water quality parameters over lakes and coastal areas and how to use STREAM application programming interface (API) to discover and download satellite images and water quality data for a selected water body. The training demonstrates how to assess changes in water quality in a given lake using QGIS. The training also demonstrates the application of a MDN model to estimate water quality parameters from satellite images.
event.host: NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training Program (ARSET)
event.learningOutcome:
By the end of this training attendees will be able to:
Identify the purpose, capabilities, and benefits of the STREAM tool for analyzing inland and coastal water bodies.
Identify the process to use STREAM to monitor chlorophyll-a concentration, Secchi disk depth, and total suspended solids in lakes and coastal waters.
Identify the steps to use STREAM API to search and download chlorophyll-a concentration, Secchi disk depth, and total suspended solids data for a specific time period.
Examine time series of chlorophyll-a concentration, Secchi disk depth, and total suspended solids using QGIS.
Identify how an open-source machine-learning model based on Mixture Density Network (MDN) enables users to estimate water quality parameters for any inland or coastal water body (greater than 100m x 100m) worldwide.
event.registrationHowto: Please register here: https://go.nasa.gov/4oZSZOm
event.targetAudience: Primary target audience: National and international water resources managers at local, state, and federal levels. Public and private water utilities, natural resources conservation organizations, and fisheries and aquaculture organizations. Secondary target audience: Academic faculty and students.
event.title: Monitoring Water Quality in Lakes and Coastal Regions Using STREAM

event.description:
Dust is one of the key components of atmospheric constituents, influencing air quality, climate, visibility, and human health. Its high spatial and temporal variability makes it difficult to monitor using surface-based observations alone, which is why spaceborne observations are essential to accurately detect, track, and monitor dust plumes across large areas.
To address these challenges, EUMETSAT provides a short course showing how its satellite-based tools respond to the current scientific needs for dust detection and visualisation.
The session begins with a brief introduction to dust, setting the scene by exploring its environmental relevance and highlighting the role of satellite Earth Observations in detecting, monitoring, and tracking dust transport.
Participants will then follow a guided demonstration on how to identify a dust event using EUMETView, EUMETSAT’s user-friendly visualisation service. This exercise will show how to generate a clear image or animation of the selected event.
The training continues with an overview of the available Jupyter Notebooks, which can be used to visualise and download Copernicus Sentinel-3 SLSTR Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) and C3S (Copernicus Climate Change Service) IASI (MAPIR Algorithm) Dust Optical Depth (DOD). The notebooks will be adapted live during the session, to demonstrate how to reproduce the same event previously identified on EUMETView, showcasing a complete workflow from visual inspection to interactive data analysis.
Resources available here -> https://classroom.eumetsat.int/course/view.php?id=596
event.learningOutcome: - Users will be familiar with EUMETSAT in the general EO industry. - Users will know which dust-related data are available from EUMETSAT/Copernicus services. - Users will independently find resources and guides related to atmospheric data, within the EUMETSAT User Portal. - Users will become familiar with the EUMETSAT visualisation tool EUMETView, and downloading tools such as EUMDAC, CDS and WEkEO (Jupyter Notebooks) - Users will become familiar with visualising dust on EUMETView and AOD and DOD using Jupyter Notebooks

event.description:
En association avec l'École Africaine de la Météorologie et de l'Aviation Civile (EAMAC) de l' Agence pour la Sécurité de la Navigation Aérienne en Afrique et à Madagascar (ASECNA), centre d'excellence de l'OMM, EUMETSAT organise une formation en présentiel sur les applications satellitaires à destination des prévisionnistes opérationnels d'Afrique de l'Ouest, d'Afrique centrale et de Madagascar.
Dispensée en français, cette formation vise à explorer les capacités de la mission Meteosat Troisième Génération (MTG). Elle mettra en évidence les avantages de MTG par rapport à MSG et montrera comment les données des instruments FCI et LI peuvent être utilisées pour améliorer la surveillance et les prévisions météorologiques. Les participants apprendront à intégrer ces données dans leurs routines opérationnelles, ce qui renforcera leurs compétences en analyse et en prévision météorologiques. Le programme comprendra également des exercices pratiques utilisant des logiciels professionnels de visualisation.
event.host: Ecole Africaine de la Météorologie et de l'Aviation Civile (EAMAC)
event.learningOutcome:
Les étudiants devraient être capables de :
• Maîtriser l'interprétation des images satellitaires MSG et MTG (RVBs). • Reconnaître la valeur ajoutée des données MTG par rapport aux données MSG. • Acquérir une expérience pratique avec les logiciels d'affichage pour les applications météorologiques. • Apprendre à intégrer les données satellitaires dans le processus de prévision opérationnelle.
event.registrationHowto: La sélection des participants au cours par EUMETSAT et l’EAMAC se fait selon les critères suivants: la priorité sera accordée aux météorologistes opérationnels ayant suivi et validé avec succès une formation en ligne récente sur les applications satellitaires organisée par EUMETSAT et ses partenaires africains, et ayant été nommés par leur Représentant Permanent auprès de l’OMM (WMO PR).

This course will address the benefits of Meteosat satellites in convective weather forecasting in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. event.description:
The field of weather forecasting is moving quickly, with AI-driven methods increasingly coming in from outside meteorology. This has created a mismatch between the background of the forecaster and the methods behind the forecast. In this talk, we will give a basic introduction to Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), with a focus on their applications in weather. The main goal is to provide insight into how these methods work and how one should reason about them, helping to bridge this gap.
This webinar will be presented by Martin Andrae and Erik Larsson (Linköping University, Sweden) on 3 February 2026 at 12:00 UTC / 13:00 CET.

event.description:
This hands-on workshop introduces participants to practical applications of AI in scientific workflows. Participants will explore how large language models can accelerate literature reviews, refine research proposals, and adapt technical material for different audiences. We will explore practical applications for data analysis, and visualization using a sample dataset.
The session also covers project organization, and preparation for job interviews. Critically, we'll address when AI use is appropriate, recognize its limitations—particularly hallucinations in literature reviews and technical writing—and develop effective prompting strategies to obtain reliable results. Through interactive exercises, participants will gain practical experience applying these tools while understanding their boundaries.
This workshop will be presented by Tsvet Ross-Lazarov (COMET) on 22 Jan 2026 at 14:00 UTC / 15:00 CET.
